title: What the Draft Conversion Practices Bill would change — and what’s at stake
label: 29 October 2026 · Joint Committee evidence session
summary: The Committee heard two panels of witnesses on the Government’s draft Conversion Practices Bill. The first panel (Stonewall, Galop and an academic) said conversion practices are real, often hidden, frequently occur in religious and pseudo‑health settings, and that the Bill should cover both efforts to change and to suppress identity, avoid an abusive/non‑abusive split, and narrow the healthcare exemption to regulated practitioners. The second panel (Gay Men’s Network, Sex Matters, LGB Alliance) warned the Bill is too broad and unclear: it risks criminalising ordinary parenting or pastoral care, chilling clinicians and schools, and raising human‑rights and legal‑certainty problems. Witnesses differed sharply about definitions, intent, healthcare exemptions, children’s cases and the best legal fixes.

chapters.title: How common are conversion practices and who is affected?
chapters.takeaway: Both panels agreed abusive conversion practices exist in the UK; they differ on how widespread they are and whether new criminal law is the best fix.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: How prevalent are conversion practices in England and Wales, and who is at risk?

turns.speaker: Stephen Kiely
turns.text: Stonewall pointed to the Government’s LGBT survey: 5% offered conversion practices, 2% underwent them; our own poll finds similar figures. Trans people, some ethnic and religious minorities, and young people are at higher risk.

turns.speaker: Kai O’Doherty
turns.text: Galop said it sees hundreds of cases each year. Their 2022 research found very high rates among trans and non‑binary people and that many practices happen in religious settings; pseudo‑healthcare and family settings also occur.

turns.speaker: Professor Ilias Trispiotis
turns.text: From international studies and UN/Council of Europe work, conversion practices are often clandestine, under‑reported and happen in many settings; other countries have acted to ban them.

turns.speaker: Dermot Kehoe
turns.text: From his LGB Alliance support groups, many callers have been confused between sexual orientation and gender identity; some detransitioners report being encouraged toward transition when they were gay, which his group sees as problematic.

turns.speaker: Dennis Kavanagh
turns.text: Gay Men’s Network warned of a particular problem in gender services where many cases showed high rates of same‑sex attraction among young clinic users; they argue this reflects an on‑the‑ground pattern of gay youth being channelled into transition.

chapters.title: What should 'conversion practices' cover?
chapters.takeaway: Supporters want both 'change' and 'suppression' covered and no benign/abusive split; critics warn the Bill’s current wording is vague and risks criminalising ordinary parenting or pastoral care.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Does the Bill’s definition include both trying to change someone and trying to persuade them not to adopt an identity?

turns.speaker: Professor Ilias Trispiotis
turns.text: The Bill covers efforts to change or influence identity, but it omits 'suppression' as a concept used elsewhere. Suppression means encouraging someone to conceal or deny their identity—other countries explicitly include it.

turns.speaker: Kai O’Doherty
turns.text: On the ground, abuse now often looks covert: people are told 'don’t show you are gay' or are isolated, surveilled or shamed—these are suppression tactics and should be in the law.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Silvertown
turns.text: Can prayer or conversations ever count? Where is the line between pastoral care and criminal conduct?

turns.speaker: Professor Ilias Trispiotis
turns.text: It depends on intent and effect. Prayer intended to change or that causes the high harm threshold could fall within the definition, but context matters and the Bill sets a high harm bar.

turns.speaker: Dennis Kavanagh
turns.text: Opponents worry the Bill criminalises parents' statements. Because it needs only an intent to change and lacks an intent‑to‑harm requirement, ordinary parental guidance could be at risk.

turns.speaker: Helen Joyce
turns.text: She agreed abusive practices exist, but warned that the Bill’s broad language could catch normal parental or professional questioning and lacks standard defences found in other criminal laws.

chapters.title: Healthcare, therapists and exemptions
chapters.takeaway: All witnesses agreed legitimate healthcare must be protected, but they disagree about how narrow or broad that protection should be.

turns.speaker: Olivia Bailey
turns.text: Could legitimate health and therapeutic care be chilled by the Bill?

turns.speaker: Stephen Kiely
turns.text: Stonewall supports a healthcare carve‑out for regulated clinicians but warned the draft is too broad and could let pseudo‑therapists escape liability; they propose limiting the exemption to practitioners regulated by statute or on a PSA‑accredited register.

turns.speaker: Lord Hope of Craighead
turns.text: Would wording like Northern Ireland’s—tying a carve‑out to regulation and compliance with professional codes—satisfy concerns?

turns.speaker: Professor Ilias Trispiotis
turns.text: Yes: other countries either list non‑conversion healthcare practices or narrow exemptions to regulated practitioners; that reassures legitimate providers while allowing prosecutions of unregulated harmful practice.

turns.speaker: Helen Joyce
turns.text: Sex Matters’ therapists warned of an existing chilling effect: many professionals already avoid gender‑distress cases because they fear complaints; training and clear, narrow carve‑outs are needed.

turns.speaker: Dennis Kavanagh
turns.text: Gay Men’s Network argued the Bill’s special focus on medical practice risks a 'deep freeze'—professionals and parents may avoid necessary conversations for fear of criminal charges.

chapters.title: Children, parents and the harm threshold
chapters.takeaway: Big disagreement: supporters say the high 'serious harm' test and coercive control precedent work; critics say the draft risks criminalising parents and lacks legal certainty.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Is there anything non‑abusive here, and how do we balance parenting duties with criminal thresholds?

turns.speaker: Professor Ilias Trispiotis
turns.text: He argued conversion practices are intrinsically discriminatory and abusive; the Bill’s harm threshold mirrors coercive control and is high, but he acknowledged proving harm can be difficult in practice.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: How would protection orders work and who would use them?

turns.speaker: Kai O’Doherty
turns.text: Galop said orders can help protect victims, modelled on forced marriage and stalking protections, but police backlogs and training gaps must be addressed for them to work.

turns.speaker: Helen Joyce
turns.text: Sex Matters warned parents and teachers could be swept in by broad wording; for example, removing a teen’s social media or setting rules might be well‑intentioned parenting but fit parts of the Bill’s funnel.

turns.speaker: Dennis Kavanagh
turns.text: He highlighted legal‑certainty and ECHR risks: the absence of an 'intent to harm' element, an undefined 'abusive' test, and possible reverse burdens could make parents unsure whether ordinary parenting is criminal.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: If refusing to affirm a child can cause distress, does that mean many parents fall within scope?

turns.speaker: Professor Ilias Trispiotis
turns.text: He reiterated the Bill’s high threshold: ordinary negative conversations would only be captured if they caused the very serious effects listed in the explanatory notes, but each case is context‑sensitive.

chapters.title: Enforcement, rights and alternatives
chapters.takeaway: Supporters want a clear criminal ban without weakening protections; critics urge targeted fixes to existing law, clearer defences, and safeguards to avoid human‑rights and chilling effects.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: If many perpetrators claim they meant well, should the Bill require proof of intent to harm?

turns.speaker: Dennis Kavanagh
turns.text: He said no intent‑to‑harm requirement plus an unclear 'abusive' test makes the offence dangerously like strict liability; he proposed amendments instead—eg, a conversion aggravation to attach to existing offences, or targeted fixes such as extending child cruelty extraterritorially.

turns.speaker: Professor Ilias Trispiotis
turns.text: He warned against a distinction between 'abusive' and 'non‑abusive' conversion practices; other jurisdictions do not use that split and it risks signalling some conversion efforts are acceptable.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Silvertown
turns.text: What about ECHR risks—freedom of expression, belief and family life?

turns.speaker: Helen Joyce
turns.text: She pointed to missing defences in the draft (reasonableness, best interests, statutory duties) and said the Bill can collide with teachers’ and employers’ duties, so carefully drafted safeguards are required.

turns.speaker: Dennis Kavanagh
turns.text: He added article 7 (law must be clear) and article 8 (family life) concerns: parents need to know the law is comprehensible; otherwise prosecutions risk incompatibility with human‑rights law.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Are protection orders useful despite implementation problems elsewhere?

turns.speaker: Kai O’Doherty
turns.text: Galop supported orders but warned they would only help if police and courts get better at recognizing conversion practices and doing risk analysis; implementation is key.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please send written follow‑up evidence if you wish; the Committee will consider definitions, the healthcare exemption, children, intent and enforcement carefully when drafting recommendations.
